title: WoundAmbit: Bridging State-of-the-Art Semantic Segmentation and Real-World Wound Care
abstract: Chronic wounds affect a large population, particularly the elderly and diabetic patients, who often exhibit limited mobility and co-existing health conditions. Automated wound monitoring via mobile image capture can reduce in-person physician visits by enabling remote tracking of wound size. Semantic segmentation is key to this process, yet wound segmentation remains underrepresented in medical imaging research. To address this, we benchmark state-of-the-art deep learning models from general-purpose vision, medical imaging, and top methods from public wound challenges. For a fair comparison, we standardize training, data augmentation, and evaluation, conducting cross-validation to minimize partitioning bias. We also assess real-world deployment aspects, including generalization to an out-of-distribution wound dataset, computational efficiency, and interpretability. Additionally, we propose a reference object-based approach to convert AI-generated masks into clinically relevant wound size estimates and evaluate this, along with mask quality, for the five best architectures based on physician assessments. Overall, the transformer-based TransNeXt showed the highest levels of generalizability. Despite variations in inference times, all models processed at least one image per second on the CPU, which is deemed adequate for the intended application. Interpretability analysis typically revealed prominent activations in wound regions, emphasizing focus on clinically relevant features. Expert evaluation showed high mask approval for all analyzed models, with VWFormer and ConvNeXtS backbone performing the best. Size retrieval accuracy was similar across models, and predictions closely matched expert annotations. Finally, we demonstrate how our AI-driven wound size estimation framework, WoundAmbit, is integrated into a custom telehealth system.

title: Towards Accurate and Lightweight Peripheral Neuroblastic Tumor Diagnosis via Contrastive Multi-scale Pathological Image Analysis
abstract: Peripheral neuroblastic tumors (pNTs) are among the most common extracranial solid tumors in children, and accurate pathological subtyping is important for risk stratification and treatment planning. However, pNT subtyping on hematoxylin-eosin whole-slide images (WSIs) remains challenging because of limited pediatric tumor cohorts, marked histological heterogeneity, inter-observer variability, and the computational burden of existing WSI classifiers. To address these challenges, we propose CoPath, a framework consisting of CoHisNet and PathVote. CoHisNet is a lightweight multi-scale feature-fusion network for patch-level histopathological classification. By replacing the multilayer perceptron components in Swin Transformer blocks and the classification head with Kolmogorov-Arnold Network layers, CoHisNet improves nonlinear feature modeling under a compact architecture. Its multi-scale interaction and contrast-driven feature-enhancement design enables the model to capture both tissue-level structures and fine-grained cellular morphology. PathVote further incorporates pathology-informed tissue-component priors to aggregate patch-level predictions into WSI-level decisions. We validated CoPath on a private two-branch PpNTs cohort and the public BreakHis breast cancer histopathology dataset. Experimental results show that CoPath achieves competitive or superior performance compared with general image classifiers, pathology foundation models under linear probing, and pathology-specific classification models, while maintaining substantially lower computational complexity. The source code is available at https://github.com/JSLiam94/CoPath.

title: Clinician-Friendly Foundation Models for Ophthalmic Image Diagnostics without Fine-Tuning or Technical Barriers
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) shows remarkable potential in medical imaging diagnostics, yet most current models require retraining when applied across different clinical settings, limiting their scalability. We developed GlobeReady, a deployment-oriented platform powered by the RetiGlobe foun- dation model and local feature augmentation. RetiGlobe was pretrained in two stages: 1) self-supervised learning using DINOv2 on 38 million synthetic ophthalmic images, and 2) contrastive learning using CLIP on 475,845 real image-text pairs spanning diverse ethnicities, imaging devices, and geographic regions worldwide. We evaluate GlobeReady on 488,448 ophthalmic images, including color fundus photographs (CFPs) and optical coherence tomography scans, from multi-centres in China, Singapore, Vietnam and the UK. Prospective testing included usability assessment with 31 ophthalmologists. Exploratory analyses evaluated domain generalisability, Bayesian uncertainty quantification, out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, and feature-based case retrieval.

title: A One-shot/Few-shot Interactive Segmentation Method for CT Image Segmentation.
abstract: Medical image ground truth annotation is important in clinical workflows for diagnosis, disease staging, prognostication of outcome, treatment planning, and treatment response assessment. However, annotating medical images requires significant human effort, especially for three-dimensional (3D) medical images. Deep learning techniques have significantly contributed to the methods of medical image annotation. Nonetheless, highly accurate automatic segmentation methods still require large-scale labeled data for training, which hinders the application in practice, especially for objects that are newly defined and/or are not well defined in the image and/or are spatially sparse with poor boundaries. Deep-learning(DL)-based interactive segmentation methods offer a trade-off between training cost and prediction performance. By leveraging extra regional prompts, these methods gain an unparalleled ability to locate the target object compared to automatic methods. This region recognition ability is essential for improving DL segmentation performance when training data are limited. In this paper, we present an interactive DL segmentation method for 3D computed tomography (CT) images, especially for the situation of one-shot/few-shot learning. Specifically, we propose a novel click prompt simulation method for training 3D interactive segmentation models inspired by the annotating procedures and focuses of human experts. The proposed prompt simulation consists of the object boundary prompt to indicate the global and local characteristics of the object and the mis-predicted region prompt to refine existing segmentations. We conduct experiments involving multiple anatomical structure segmentation tasks on our publicly available abdomen dataset under the condition of one-shot/few-shot learning. The experimental results demonstrate that the interactive segmentation method is more efficacious than its fully automated counterpart, which highlights the significant potential of applying interactive segmentation methods on the condition of lacking training data.

title: Prediction of Disease Quantification via PET/CT Images and Auto-Segmentation of Target Objects.
abstract: In this paper, we propose a deep learning-based disease quantification (DQ) method which predicts object-level total lesion burden (TLB) of target objects from segmentations derived by automatic methods on PET/CT images. Our approach employs a U-Net shaped network using CT images, standardized SUV images, and delineated object mask as three-channel input, and predicted segmentation mask and lesion map (LM) as two-channel output. Ground truth LM is generated based on normality distribution of metabolic activities of the object, and the loss function is a weighted sum of segmentation loss, LM loss, and TLB loss. We evaluated the method on clinical datasets comprising 58 PET/CT scans, covering five organs and five lymph node zones. 3-fold cross-validation experiments were conducted using both manual and auto-segmented masks. Results show that the proposed method achieves clinically acceptable errors, where half of experiments showed errors below 15% and most of the remainder with errors under 30%. Our method demonstrates a solution for automated DQ from PET/CT images, potentially reducing manual effort while maintaining clinically meaningful accuracy and reproducibility.

title: Anatomically ROI- and IOI-informed Hybrid U-Net model for Abdominal Object Segmentation in CT images.
abstract: Segmentation in medical imaging is a critical and challenging task, essential for improved disease diagnosis, staging, treatment planning, and response assessment. Over the years, various deep learning (DL) methods have been developed to enhance image segmentation. Among these, encoder-decoder methods, particularly the U-Net model and its variants, have proven effective in medical image segmentation. These methods incrementally address the limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in recognizing high-level object concepts by integrating different-level features. We add natural intelligence (NI) into AI and leverage anatomical knowledge to further improve object segmentation accuracy. Our study introduces the hybrid U-Net (HUN) model that focuses on regions of interest (ROI) and intensities of interest (IOI) determined by NI, thus enhancing resource utilization efficiency and reducing irrelevant information. The HUN model balances local and global feature extraction, improving segmentation outcomes in 15 of 16 objects of interest in abdominal low-dose CT images compared to the U-Net. The novel concept of hybrid intelligence (HI), which combines NI with AI/DL techniques, is explored, showcasing its robustness and generalizability across various medical imaging applications. Our findings underscore the importance of incorporating NI into AI-driven medical imaging methods, paving the way for more effective and reliable solutions in medical image analysis and holding significant potential for improving patient care and clinical outcomes.

title: Body composition analysis: Single slice vs. volumetric measures.
abstract: Body composition analysis (BCA) is useful for evaluating nutritional status, general health, and predicting patient outcomes. Computed tomography (CT)-based BCA has become increasingly popular, with research often focusing on single-transaxial-slice measurements at the L3 vertebral level to estimate volumetric tissue properties. This method assumes the same tissue distribution in all transaxial slices across the body, potentially leading to inaccuracies in clinical assessments. This retrospective study investigates the reliability of single-slice BCA compared to volumetric measurements across the torso in a cohort of 237 adults. Using the GA-Net architecture for automatic tissue segmentation, we analyzed tissue distribution at 25 craniocaudal levels. Our results reveal significant variability in tissue distribution, with cross-sectional areas at L3 poorly correlating with 3D tissue volumes. For instance, we observed a visceral adipose tissue (VAT) volume difference of over 2,900 cm 3 between two subjects with similar L3 VAT areas. These findings indicate that single-slice BCA, particularly at L3, is insufficient for accurate body composition analysis. This study underscores the need for more precise, volumetric approaches to BCA, which would enhance the accuracy of clinical assessments, disease prognostication, and treatment planning.
